summary.summary: Oldham's 2024/25 outturn shows total borrowing up 29.6% in the year, from £181.110m to £234.817m, as the Capital Financing Requirement grew £70.859m to £559.839m. The council breached the PFI/finance-lease element of its Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit during the year (driven by an IFRS 16 recalculation of PFI lease liabilities) and is asking members to raise both limits rather than reduce the exposure. £39m of LOBO loans carried call dates within the following 12 months; a £5m LOBO with FMS Wertmanagement was called on 31 March 2025 at a proposed 7.67% rate and the council repaid it in full on 7 April 2025. Financing costs as a share of net revenue stream rose from 6.50% to 7.61% year-on-year.

signals.headline: The PFI/finance-lease element of the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit was breached in 2024/25 (£223.812m against a £183.5m/£186.0m boundary/limit); Cabinet is asked to raise both to £230.0m/£235.0m rather than cut the exposure.
signals.why: A breached limit resolved by raising the ceiling, not reducing debt, is exactly the pattern this signal is designed to flag.

signals.headline: Total borrowing rose 29.6% in the year, from £181.110m to £234.817m (+£53.707m), almost all of it in short-term borrowing.
signals.why: A rapid rise in gross debt within a single year is worth watching for pace and refinancing implications.

signals.headline: £39m of LOBO loans had call dates within 12 months of 31 March 2025; a £5m LOBO with FMS Wertmanagement was called at 31 March 2025 (proposed rate 7.67%) and repaid in full on 7 April 2025.
signals.why: LOBO call windows can force refinancing at short notice and at rates set by the lender, not the council.

signals.headline: Financing costs as a share of net revenue stream rose from 6.50% (2023/24) to 7.61% (2024/25), as financing costs increased from £19.424m to £26.252m.
signals.why: Debt-servicing is taking a growing bite out of the revenue budget.

news_drafts.headline: Oldham forecasts £21.048m schools deficit for 2026/27 after £6.254m government grant
news_drafts.lead:
Oldham Council forecasts a cumulative deficit of £21.048m on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) at the end of 2026/27, after £6.254m of High Needs Sustainability Grant. Before the grant the figure was £27.302m, according to the quarter 2 revenue monitor. The high needs block, the part of school funding for special educational needs and disabilities, is forecast to overspend by £20.206m for the year, and £6.949m was brought forward from 2025/26.

The Department for Education has accepted the council's SEND Reform Plan and the grant, which the paper describes as a 90% reimbursement of the agreed annual deficit through to 31 March 2028. The paper says the statutory override, the temporary rule that keeps such a deficit off the main balance sheet, ends at that date, after which any deficit will offset general usable reserves.

The reform plan sets out indicative spend of £2.15m and aims to cut independent placements by 10–30% over three years, from 118 at the fourth quarter of 2025/26 to 85 by year three. Inclusion base places are to rise from 80 to 363. The meeting also has a decision report seeking £200k of capital works at Latics Zone, Boundary Park, for alternative provision, funded from the high needs capital grant, which has a £8.310m unallocated balance. The plan's risk register rates delays to inclusion bases and specialist provision as critical in impact, likely, and red.
news_drafts.paper_title: Revenue Monitor and Capital Investment Programme 2026-27 - Quarter 2 FINAL

news_drafts.headline: Oldham's high needs capital grant allocations for 2021-24 total £6,031,837, up from £830,009 in 2021-22
news_drafts.lead:
Oldham's SEND and Inclusion Strategy reports that the council's allocations of high needs provision capital grant from the Department for Education for 2021-24 total £6,031,837. The 2021-22 allocation was £830,009. The year-by-year split is £830,009 for 2021-22, £2,189,364 for 2022-23 and £3,012,464 for 2023-24. The strategy, put to the Governance, Strategy and Resources Scrutiny Board on 22 October 2026, says the paper's text rounds the total to "6.0m (from the original 0.8m allocated in 2021-22)". The council says the grant for 2022-23 and 2023-24 will allow more sufficiency projects to proceed and add specialist places in the borough.

High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The strategy says the Delivering Better Value programme will support "a more targeted budget" for specific identified areas. It places monitoring of independent non-maintained special school placements within the ongoing dedicated schools grant (DSG) sustainability improvement programme. The DSG is the government grant that funds schools. The strategy states an intention to assure value for money to achieve financial balance.

A separate SEND Reform Plan says the council moved £7.247m from the Schools Block to the High Needs Block across the five financial years 2016/17 to 2020/21. It states: "The Council is not currently contemplating such a transfer in 2026/27." Any future transfer would focus on SEND reform activity that reduces future demand on specialist provision, and would need Schools Forum approval. The plan says the programme team is supported by "some roles funded through the Transformation grant".

news_drafts.headline: Oldham faces £39m refinancing wall as costly loan calls mount
news_drafts.lead: Oldham Council faces an immediate refinancing challenge, with £39m of LOBO loans (bank borrowing where lenders can force early repayment at new rates) set to come due within the next 12 months. Two such loans were called this year at 7.67% and 6.70% respectively—240 to 340 basis points above the council's existing portfolio average of 4.33%. The looming calls represent half of Oldham's £75.5m LOBO portfolio, with counterparties including Dexia Finance and KBC Bank. Net borrowing meanwhile has risen 12.5% in one year to £210.7m, and the council is deliberately deferring external borrowing pending better market conditions while reserves are forecast to decline to £129.9m by March 2027.

findings.committee: Governance, Strategy and Resources Scrutiny Board
findings.paper_title: 020 - Principal Decision Report - Latic Zone – High Needs Provisions Capital Allocation (HNPCA)
findings.headline: Jamieson Contracting Limited's lowest-cost tender for the Latics Zone refurbishment is £133,507.27 excl. VAT, against up to £200k of previously approved HNPCA funding.
findings.detail: The paper reports eight compliant bids, with Jamieson Contracting Limited submitting the lowest cost after moderation. The contract price is set against the £200k capital funding previously approved for the scheme. The paper's risks section notes that cost overruns above the contract sum are to be monitored by the School Capital Project Manager and Capital Finance Manager.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing a tendered contract price with an approved capital envelope can see the headroom on a scheme and the risk that programme delay could push works outside the DfE HNPCA allocation.
findings.figures: £133,507.27 excl. VAT; £160,208.72 incl. VAT; up to £200k approved HNPCA funding; eight bidders
findings.quote: Capital Funding has been previously approved for this scheme of up to £200k

findings.committee: Governance, Strategy and Resources Scrutiny Board
findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitor and Capital Investment Programme 2026-27 - Quarter 2 FINAL
findings.headline: The Council is taking this report as an emergency decision by the Chief Executive under the delegation for emergency executive decisions.
findings.detail: The paper states that the Cabinet must review the revenue position under section 28 of the Local Government Act 2023 and approve capital virements. The Monitoring Officer's comments say the Council has not yet appointed a Leader or Deputy Leader for the current municipal year, after failing at successive meetings to do so.
findings.matters: A council operating with no appointed Leader or Deputy Leader, and taking capital and revenue decisions by emergency officer delegation, is a governance position that lenders and peer councils would want to note.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitor and Capital Investment Programme 2026-27 - Quarter 2 FINAL
findings.headline: Resources forecasts a (£1.195m) favourable variance, from (£0.309m) at Quarter 1, driven by vacant post slippage.
findings.detail: The paper says the favourable position is partly offset by a £0.177m pressure in Commissioning & Procurement from agency cover for vacant posts. A restructure is under way that the paper says is expected to remove the reliance on agency staff.
findings.matters: Vacancy underspends are a common source of in-year favourable variances, and the paper states they are offset in part by agency costs, which finance directors elsewhere would want to see reconciled.
findings.figures: (£1.195m) Quarter 2 favourable variance; (£0.309m) Quarter 1 variance; £0.177m Commissioning & Procurement pressure
findings.quote: The key driver for this forecast favourable position is due to slippage on vacant posts across the directorate as a whole

findings.committee: Governance, Strategy and Resources Scrutiny Board
findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitor and Capital Investment Programme 2026-27 - Quarter 2 FINAL
findings.headline: The Council has received £6.410m of usable capital receipts in-year against a 2026/27 financing requirement of £4.164m.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme depends on a small number of large receipts, and that delay would create a pressure. Table 5 shows over-programming of £5.313m in 2026/27, rising to £7.946m in 2027/28, which the paper says it is retaining for now. If receipts fall, the paper says the gap would be met by more prudential borrowing or a smaller programme.
findings.matters: Capital receipts that are over-programmed against the financing requirement, and the switch to borrowing if they fall, is a funding risk that lenders and peer finance teams track closely.
findings.figures: £6.410m received in-year; £4.164m 2026/27 financing requirement; £3.067m identified in-year; £5.313m 2026/27 over-programming; £7.946m 2027/28 over-programming
findings.quote: The total net usable capital receipts currently received in year is £6.410m

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitor and Capital Investment Programme 2026-27 - Quarter 2 FINAL
findings.headline: The 2026/27 Capital Programme is revised to £109.809m, with £24.307m spent to 30 September 2026, 22.14% of the forecast outturn.
findings.detail: The paper says the spend profile is marginally higher than last year's 21.25%. An annual review of the programme is under way to identify surplus resources and any further rephasing, and the paper states that the outturn currently matches the budget.
findings.matters: A capital programme revised upward by £7.347m mid-year, with a review of rephasing and receipts under way, is a scheme-level risk that other councils' capital teams can benchmark.
findings.figures: £109.809m revised 2026/27 programme; £102.464m original programme; £24.307m spend to 30 September 2026; 22.14% of forecast outturn; 21.25% last year
